transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
Lately I keep thinking my family might be better off without me, and those thoughts are starting to scare me. It's really hard for me to admit, but I just don't know how to make them stop.
Have you ever experienced periods of feeling this down or depressed in the past, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

I've had these heavy, down periods before, and also times where I felt the exact opposite—really revved up with big plans. These swings have been coming and going for several years now. But this current stretch is by far the worst it has ever been.
During those 'revved up' times, how long did that high-energy feeling typically last, and did it ever cause serious trouble in your daily life or relationships?

Those high-energy periods usually lasted for a few weeks at a time. They did cause some strain, as I'd get really snappy and irritated with my wife and kids when they tried to get me to slow down or pointed out that my numbers didn't add up. I also struggled to actually finish my workshop orders because I was so restless, though the worst of the business trouble always hit when I crashed.

During your past down periods, did you experience a deep sadness or loss of interest in almost all activities that lasted for at least two weeks straight, along with changes in sleep, appetite, or energy?

Yes, during those down times I feel a deep, heavy sadness and completely lose interest in everything, even my woodworking and salsa dancing. These periods last much longer than two weeks—this current one has been dragging on for about six months now. I also feel constantly exhausted and completely drained of energy, no matter how much I sleep.
During those high-energy periods, did you ever need to be hospitalized, or did you experience highly unusual beliefs, like having special powers, that others found completely unrealistic?

No, I’ve never been hospitalized during those high times. I didn't think I had literal superpowers, but I did have this intense, unrealistic confidence where I felt like I had a special gift and could easily turn my little workshop into a famous online brand to show everyone how it's done.

During those high-energy periods, did you ever make impulsive decisions or engage in risky behaviors—like major spending sprees or reckless investments—that caused serious, lasting trouble for you or your family?

No, I never really went on big spending sprees or made reckless financial investments during those times. Instead, I just poured all of that restless energy into staying up until two or three in the morning planning, sketching, and redesigning the workshop.

During those high-energy times, did your behavior ever cause a complete breakdown in your ability to work or manage your daily life, or were you always able to keep things running despite the restlessness?

During those high-energy times, I didn't have a complete breakdown, though I was extremely scattered—pacing around the shop and starting multiple projects without actually finishing them. The actual breakdown where I couldn't manage my work, pay bills, or handle daily life only happened once I crashed into this heavy, low mood.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's clinical history describes recurrent major depressive episodes and past hypomanic episodes. The current episode is a severe depressive episode lasting six months, characterized by profound sadness, anhedonia, fatigue, and suicidal ideation, resulting in severe functional impairment. The past elevated periods lasted several weeks and were characterized by increased energy, decreased need for sleep, irritability, and grandiosity, but did not cause severe functional impairment, require hospitalization, or involve psychotic features, which fits the definition of hypomania rather than mania. Under ICD-10, Bipolar II disorder (recurrent depressive and hypomanic episodes) is classified under F31.8 (Other bipolar affective disorders), whereas F31.4 is typically reserved for Bipolar I disorder current episode severe depression.
